solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Project I stuck to furiously

indicators.note: doing something furiously means doing it wildly and without order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter as the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to having worked on a project in a frenzy, never letting go of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project' reads as a noun, a piece of work, but it is the verb: to jut out from a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To project is to protrude beyond a surface, which is the phrasal verb meaning jut or extend outward.

clue.text: Basis of philosophy exists with every single PM

parts.note: the Tao, 'the way', is the foundation of Taoist philosophy
to exist is simply to be: 'it is'
each means every single one taken individually

explanation.surface: A grand claim that one philosophical principle underlies every prime minister there has ever been.
explanation.walkthrough: The Taoiseach is the title of the Irish prime minister; the Irish word is spelt with an unexpected run of vowels, which the three plain pieces build for you.
explanation.definitionFit: PM abbreviates prime minister, and the Taoiseach is the head of government in the Republic of Ireland.

clue.text: Senior footballer better practise with no end of vigour

parts.note: to cap a story is to better or outdo it

indicators.note: 'no' says the following item is absent, so it is taken away from the word beside it

parts.note: to practise for an event is to train

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of vigour, which comes out of the practising word

explanation.surface: Advice that an older footballer should train harder, without slacking in energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like an adjective but it is the verb, to top or cap. Removing the final R of vigour from TRAIN leaves TAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The captain leads the team on the pitch, so is the senior player in rank among the eleven footballers.

clue.text: Different source that has given away millions

indicators.note: whatever has been given away is no longer held, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: a mother is the origin or source of something, as in 'the mother of all battles'
M is the standard abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A philanthropic fund, unlike the rest, that has donated millions.
explanation.walkthrough: Mother as 'source' is the stretch here: necessity is the mother of invention. Its M goes, leaving the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Other means not the same one, distinct or alternative, which is what different conveys as an adjective.

clue.text: Animal found in middle of mountains, say

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so that single letter alone is taken

parts.note: mountains has nine letters and the fifth sits at the centre
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say, an apple'

explanation.surface: A wild creature that lives up in the mountain heights, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: A teg is a sheep in its second year, before its first shearing; it is a crossword regular despite being rare elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A teg is a young sheep, so it is one specific example of the general category of farm livestock creatures.

clue.text: Darn discomfort caused by exercise?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mend cloth with needle and thread
second meaning: a sharp pain in the side that comes on while running

explanation.surface: A grumbling 'darn!' at the aches that follow a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darn' passes as a mild curse, but it is the sewing verb; the question mark marks the second half as a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewing a repair is stitching, and a sudden side cramp during running is also called by that same word.

clue.text: Person finally sick of dancing with a partner?

indicators.note: dancers move around and change places, so the letters swap positions

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word beside it

parts.note: the final letter of sick
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who has finally had enough of dancing alongside a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' seems to modify the whole phrase, but it reaches only one word. The question mark flags a definition that needs a moment's thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone already in a relationship is described as taken or claimed, an idiom for being unavailable to other suitors.

clue.text: Temporary current running through place underground close to dam

indicators.note: something that runs through passes into the middle of what it crosses, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: to inter is to bury, putting a body in the ground
I is the symbol for electric current in physics

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of dam

explanation.surface: A makeshift water flow channelled through an underground site near a dam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' and 'dam' set up a hydro scene; current is just I, and 'place underground' is a verb phrase meaning bury.
explanation.definitionFit: Interim means for the time being, a provisional arrangement lasting only until something permanent replaces it.

clue.text: Company taking over empty neighbourhood building in LA

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so the other piece goes within

parts.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its insides, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of neighbourhood
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A developer buys up a deserted neighbourhood block in Los Angeles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking over' looks like one phrase meaning acquiring, but it splits: 'taking' holds, and 'over' is the cricket O.
explanation.definitionFit: A condo, short for condominium, is the American term for an apartment block whose units are individually owned.

clue.text: Method initially introduced to get free ticket

indicators.note: to be introduced to something is to be put into it, so one piece enters another

parts.note: to cop is slang for to get or catch, as in 'cop a look'

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter is the one taken

parts.note: the opening letter of method

explanation.surface: A trick for wangling a freebie seat at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' sounds like part of the scheme for obtaining the ticket, but it is slang for catch, as in 'cop a glimpse', and the initial goes in the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A comp is short for complimentary ticket, one handed out without charge to guests or reviewers.

clue.text: Husband stupidly cheating claims love is intense

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogies

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so one letter is held inside the others
acting stupidly means behaving without sense, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A foolish unfaithful husband insists his passion is overwhelming.
explanation.walkthrough: The O for love goes into the jumbled letters of cheating, and the whole lot follows the H.
explanation.definitionFit: High-octane fuel is powerful, so the term is used figuratively for anything forceful, energetic or dynamic.

clue.text: Training on F1 track, wearing extremely expensive footwear

indicators.note: whatever wears something has it around it, so one piece is enclosed
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of expensive

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another follows it, so the pieces sit in sequence

parts.note: Spa-Francorchamps in Belgium hosts the Formula One Belgian Grand Prix
drill is repeated practice or training, as in a military exercise

explanation.surface: A racing driver doing practice laps at a Grand Prix circuit in pricey shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expensive footwear' wants to be the definition; the adjective is only there to supply its outer letters, and 'footwear' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: An espadrille is a canvas shoe with a rope sole, so it is one particular kind of light summer shoe.

clue.text: Liberal German certainly not upset to be featured in warrant

indicators.note: featuring in something means appearing inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to warrant is to permit or allow, which is to let

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: nein is German for no, an emphatic 'certainly not'

explanation.surface: A permissive German who flatly refuses to be distressed at being named in an arrest warrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The German 'no' reads upward in the down light, and sits between the E and T of LET.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal here means tolerant and indulgent, generous in allowing freedom, which is what a merciful, permissive person shows.

clue.text: Cross threshold on the way back

indicators.note: going back retraces the route in the opposite direction, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: the threshold is the entrance to a room, standing for the door itself

explanation.surface: Stepping over a doorstep as you come home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as a verb, to step over, but it is the noun. A rood is the crucifix, especially one above a church's rood screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A rood is an old word for the crucifix on which Christ died, the Christian cross, as in Holyrood.

clue.text: Continue leading cheers at home

parts.note: main means chief or principal, the leading one
ta is British informal thanks, like 'cheers'
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Keep leading the celebrations in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' as a toast suggests drinking, but in British speech it also means thanks, which is the everyday 'ta'.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain something is to keep it going or sustain it without interruption, so it carries the sense of continuing.

clue.text: Love helping to support a party

indicators.note: in a down clue what supports sits below, so the pieces stack in that order

parts.note: taken as written
a do is an informal word for a party
a helping is a portion, and a ration is a measured portion

explanation.surface: Someone who loves pitching in to back a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' looks like a verb but it is the noun, a serving of food. 'Party' suggests politics; here it is a social do.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoration is deep devotion and worship, so it is a strong synonym for the noun meaning great affection.

clue.text: Encourage female not to lose face when interrupted by guys

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into the middle, so another piece goes inside
a face is the front, so losing it means dropping the first letter

parts.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
taken as written
guys are men

explanation.surface: Urging a woman to keep her dignity when men keep butting in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not to lose face' reads as an idiom about dignity; it is an instruction to drop the N of not.
explanation.definitionFit: To foment is to stir up or instigate trouble, so it means to encourage, usually something unwelcome like unrest.

clue.text: New person left out? It almost happens!

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: whatever is out has been removed or excluded, so the letter goes

parts.note: an earthling is a human, as aliens might call one
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A newcomer is shut out of the group and nearly has a breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: Person as EARTHLING is the stretch: it is how a science-fiction alien would address a human.
explanation.definitionFit: A near thing is a narrow escape, an event that very nearly occurred, so the whole exclamation describes it in a phrase.

clue.text: Starts to seem highly engrossed by Eastern faith

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of seem and highly
someone engrossed by a hobby is really into it

explanation.surface: A newcomer starts to look deeply absorbed in an Asian religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engrossed by' looks like a container instruction, but it is the plain synonym, the informal 'into'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, so it is one specific example of an Eastern religious belief system.

clue.text: Manage to be upstanding and celebrate work in the NHS?

indicators.note: standing upright in a down clue means reading from the bottom upwards, so letters reverse

parts.note: to manage a business is to run it
to sing is to celebrate in song, as in 'sing his praises'

explanation.surface: A rousing call to stand up and cheer the people who work in Britain's health service.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's National Health Service; the question mark warns that nursing is just one example of work done there.
explanation.definitionFit: Caring for patients as a nurse is a typical job in the National Health Service, so it is one example of health work.

clue.text: Welshman acquires rigging equipment from Scotland perhaps

indicators.note: to acquire something is to take it into your possession, so one piece is held within

parts.note: Euan is a man's name, the anglicised form of the Welsh Ieuan
a ship's rigging is made of rope

explanation.surface: A man from Wales buys sailing tackle that perhaps came from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From Scotland perhaps' looks like it describes the gear, but it is the definition by example; the perhaps signals that.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland lies in Europe, so a Scot is one instance of someone belonging to that continent.

clue.text: Musician's track mostly introduces a new one

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so the other pieces go inside
mostly means nearly all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a piste is a ski run or track
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A band member's latest recording brings in a fresh song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musician's track' reads as a song on an album; the apostrophe-s is 'is', and the track is a ski slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A pianist plays the piano, so is one particular kind of instrumental performer.

clue.text: Small, standard box?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
par is the standard or norm, as in golf

explanation.surface: A query about an ordinary small-sized carton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container noun; it is the verb, to fight with fists, and the question mark admits the sparring is only practice.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to practise boxing with a partner, exchanging light punches in training rather than a real fight.

clue.text: At first, pet Alsatian regularly rejected carb-heavy food

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter of pet

indicators.note: throwing out letters at regular intervals leaves every other one standing

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of Alsatian

explanation.surface: A pet dog turns its nose up at starchy food at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' suggests a reversal, but here it means discarded: every other letter of Alsatian is thrown away. An Alsatian is the British name for a German shepherd dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is made from wheat flour, so it is a carbohydrate-rich staple, the kind of meal athletes load up on.

clue.text: Travelling pretty far to take in a later, exclusive event

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it within, so one letter goes inside
travelling means moving about, so these letters shift into new positions

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written

explanation.surface: Making a long journey to attend a late-night, invitation-only gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The single A is taken into the rearranged letters of 'pretty far'.
explanation.definitionFit: An after-party follows a main event, often a premiere or concert, with only invited guests admitted, so it is later and select.

clue.text: Many papers covering large area of study

indicators.note: a cover goes over and around something, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a ream is 500 sheets of paper
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A pile of academic papers spanning a broad field of research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests essays or newspapers, but it is sheets of paper counted in reams.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a domain or sphere, used figuratively for a field of knowledge, as in 'the realm of physics'.

clue.text: Apiarists haphazardly grabbing top of dying plant

indicators.note: to grab something is to seize and hold it, so one letter is held inside
done haphazardly means done without order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of dying

explanation.surface: Careless beekeepers seize the tip of a wilting flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dying plant' wants to be read together; dying only supplies its D. The aspidistra was a famously hardy Victorian parlour plant.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspidistra is a leafy evergreen houseplant of the lily family, so it is an example of a plant.

clue.text: Heavy weight cask picked up

indicators.note: a sound picked up is caught by the ear, so the clue works by sound rather than spelling

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: A weighty barrel is hoisted off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' suits lifting a heavy barrel, but it means heard. A tun is a big brewer's cask.
explanation.definitionFit: A ton is a unit of mass of about a thousand kilograms, so it is a large measure of weight.

clue.text: Definitely somewhat still able to win

indicators.note: somewhat means partly, so only part of the neighbouring word is used

parts.note: the letters run inside the middle of the word

explanation.surface: A competitor who is surely, to a degree, still in contention.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the fourth to seventh letters of Definitely; 'somewhat' looks like a hedge on the claim.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor who is in it remains in contention, the idiom for having a chance of victory.

clue.text: Prohibition all but ended? Correct!

indicators.note: all but means everything except the final part, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition
something ended is over and gone

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Prohibition has nearly finished, and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: Prohibition with its capital suggests the American alcohol ban era; it is just a ban. Bang on is British slang for exactly right.
explanation.definitionFit: Bang on is a British informal exclamation meaning exactly right or spot on, used to agree emphatically.

clue.text: Means of identifying bugs cracked by social media firm

indicators.note: something cracked open has another thing break into it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: to bug someone is to annoy or nag them
Meta is the company that owns Facebook and Instagram

explanation.surface: A method of detecting insects, or listening devices, that a tech giant has worked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' suggests insects or spying devices; it is the verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: Name tags are badges worn at events showing who someone is, so they serve to identify their wearers.
